items.title: Two active magma reservoirs may lie beneath Masaya volcano, near 2 million people
items.desc: Masaya volcano in Nicaragua sits within 13 miles (21 kilometers) of 2 million people and is a popular tourist destination due to its lava lake. Penn State researchers recently found evidence of two new magma sources under the active volcano, highlighting what they called the critical importance of understanding transitions in volcanic behavior and shallow magma processes, especially when they potentially pose hazards to local communities.

items.desc: EPFL researchers have developed a chip-based laser that keeps a very stable frequency across its tested operating range, without needing active electronic control. Their research is published in the journal Nature Photonics.

items.title: The vanishing of aurochs: Genetic evidence reveals multiple stressors at the same time
items.desc: Aurochs, the ancient ancestors of modern cattle, once roamed large parts of Europe, Asia and northern Africa. New research by an international team led by Lund University indicates that multiple factors contributed to their demise in northern Europe—one of the first areas where they became extinct.

items.desc: Neutron stars, the extremely dense remains of massive stars that exploded at the end of their lives, are widely studied astrophysical objects. Some of these stars, known as pulsars, spin and send out beams of radio waves, making them appear to pulse as the beams sweep past Earth.

items.title: Bushfire simulation reveals green strategy that could cut Australia's fire threat
items.desc: New modeling shows irrigating low-flammability vegetation substantially reduces the predicted spread and intensity of wildfires, which could give communities critical extra preparation time, according to a University of the Sunshine Coast study.

items.title: Study links hurricane exposure to higher eviction risk for renters
items.desc: Hurricanes can displace renters even when their homes suffer no damage, according to new research led by Rowan University urban planner Qian He.

items.title: The economy is resilient: Why do many Americans feel differently? An expert explains
items.desc: Even as the Federal Reserve moves to raise interest rates for the first time in three years, many of the metrics that economists rely on to gauge the overall health of the economy—like jobs reports, the unemployment rate and the stock market—have looked relatively strong in recent months. Despite this, only about 24% of Americans rated the economy as "good" or "excellent" in a recent Pew Research Center survey.

items.title: Q&A: How can marketers use AI effectively—without losing human judgment?
items.desc: As marketers increasingly turn to artificial intelligence (AI) tools to create content and improve the efficiency of their workflows, a new study by a Penn State researcher and collaborators proposes an approach to deploying AI-generated marketing content at scale while reducing the need for costly and time-consuming traditional testing.

items.title: This diet may slow brain aging by 2.5 years
items.desc: People who followed the MIND diet more closely showed slower brain shrinkage and less grey matter loss over time, with the strongest differences equivalent to about 2.5 years of delayed brain aging. Berries and poultry were linked with healthier brain changes, while sweets and fried fast foods were associated with greater tissue loss.

items.title: Alzheimer’s risk gene APOE4 may have a reversible weakness
items.desc: The Alzheimer’s risk gene APOE4 may actively damage brain blood vessels and sabotage the cellular systems that remove harmful proteins. Researchers were able to reverse some of these effects in experiments, revealing promising new targets for Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s, and other neurodegenerative diseases.

items.title: Could quitting ultra-processed food boost your mental health?
items.desc: People with depression who dramatically cut ultra-processed foods experienced notable improvements in their symptoms in a small preliminary study. Researchers suspect healthier eating may benefit the brain partly by reducing gut damage and chronic inflammation.

items.title: This giant stick insect fooled scientists for decades
items.desc: Scientists have identified two new species of large Australian stick insects, including one that lays extraordinary “lidded” eggs never before recorded in the group. The discovery also revealed that a familiar stick insect had been misidentified for decades, showing how much biodiversity may still be hiding in plain sight.

items.title: Watch Live: NASA’s Crew-13 could make the fastest U.S. trip to the ISS ever
items.desc: NASA’s SpaceX Crew-13 mission is scheduled to launch four astronauts to the International Space Station on October 1. The Dragon could reach the orbiting laboratory in just 7 hours and 50 minutes, making it the fastest U.S. spacecraft journey to the ISS in history.

items.title: This new qubit could be 100 times less error-prone in superfluid quantum computer breakthrough
items.desc: A proposed qubit made with superfluid helium could cut quantum computing error rates by around 100 times by shielding quantum information from common forms of electromagnetic noise. If experiments confirm the predictions, the technology could eventually work alongside today’s superconducting qubits or serve as a new kind of quantum memory.

items.title: New “plant armor” more than triples strawberry yields
items.desc: A new protective fabric boosted strawberry yields by as much as 3.56 times while blocking insects and still allowing sunlight, rain, and airflow to reach the plants. Originally inspired by research on military clothing, Plant Armor could also help farms reduce pesticide and water use.

items.title: Cannabis users were twice as likely to commit violence, review finds
items.desc: A review of more than 265,000 people found that cannabis use was associated with higher rates of both committing violence and becoming a victim of it. The researchers say the link is significant but does not prove cannabis itself is the cause.

items.title: A record-breaking X-ray flash may reveal the birth of a magnetar
items.desc: Astronomers have found strong evidence that some mysterious, minutes-long X-ray flashes are produced when two neutron stars collide and create a magnetar. One record-setting event glowed in X-rays for nearly 10 minutes, potentially opening a new way to find these extreme cosmic mergers.

items.title: Quantum teleportation breakthrough: Scientists crack a 25-year entanglement challenge
items.desc: Scientists have developed and experimentally demonstrated a long-sought method for identifying W states, an important form of multi-photon quantum entanglement. The technique could make complex entangled systems much easier to measure, opening new possibilities for quantum teleportation, communication, and computing.

items.title: Sharks can hear nearly 250 feet away and pinpoint the source
items.desc: Wild blacktip sharks can detect low-frequency sounds from nearly 250 feet away, according to experiments conducted off the Florida coast. The sharks not only heard the sounds but sharply changed direction away from them, suggesting they could pinpoint where they were coming from.

items.title: Bats may have first evolved in Europe 65 million years ago
items.desc: A huge genomic and fossil study suggests bats first evolved in Europe around 65 to 60 million years ago before spreading across the globe. The findings also indicate that flight and echolocation emerged near the beginning of bat evolution, potentially helping explain how bats became one of the most successful mammal groups on Earth.

items.title: The ice blasting from Saturn's moon Enceladus is stranger than scientists realized
items.desc: Enceladus may naturally separate and concentrate chemicals from its hidden ocean as droplets slowly freeze and shatter on their way into space. The process could explain Cassini’s puzzling ice-grain chemistry while giving future spacecraft a powerful advantage in searching for organic compounds and clues to life.

items.title: This common mistake can add nearly 7 points to your blood pressure reading
items.desc: A common mistake during blood pressure checks could make readings appear substantially higher than they really are. Johns Hopkins researchers found that leaving the arm unsupported can raise systolic readings by about 6.5 mmHg, potentially affecting a hypertension diagnosis.

items.title: NASA’s Curiosity rover just hit 5,000 days on Mars and sent back this stunning view
items.desc: NASA’s Curiosity rover marked 5,000 Martian days by capturing morning and afternoon views that were blended into a striking Mars “postcard.” The panorama shows Curiosity, its tracks, and the enormous landscape surrounding Mount Sharp and Gale Crater.

items.title: Why Is the Global Economy So Resilient?
items.desc: With the global economy having weathered major trade and energy shocks over the past two years, growth should improve in 2027, and inflation should fall. Although various political and policy-driven risks could change the outlook, they remain less likely than the relatively benign baseline scenario.

items.title: Closing Europe’s Dynamism Deficit
items.desc: Europe has built an economic framework that protects yesterday’s champions at the expense of tomorrow’s potential winners. To remain competitive, sovereign, and secure in the 21st century, it will need a new model geared toward promoting domestic innovation and commercialization at scale.

items.title: America’s Looming Debt Reckoning
items.desc: High debt levels become dangerous when rising interest rates push up borrowing costs and governments fail to respond. With little political appetite to rein in its federal deficit and ballooning debt, the United States risks finding itself with few options when the next war, recession, or financial crisis arrives.

items.title: The OECD Should Be Reclaimed, Not Abandoned
items.desc: In recent years, the OECD has strayed from its core mission of coordinating economic policy among the US and its allies, instead building programs around gender budgeting and environmental justice. The Trump administration should use its leverage at the organization to return its focus to economics and national security.

items.title: Putin Is Testing NATO at Ukraine’s Borders
items.desc: The Kremlin is determined to isolate Ukraine, which means not only breaking the will of the country’s backers, but also cutting it off physically by striking merchant ships, ports, and border crossings. These assaults cannot go unanswered, because they embolden Russian President Vladimir Putin to continue testing the West.

items.title: The Hard Road to a Middle-Power Order
items.desc: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has challenged the world’s middle powers to build a better international order. Yet they are increasingly turning to coalitions of the willing and a patchwork of separate initiatives that risk entrenching zero-sum mindsets and making collective action harder.

items.title: The Sovereign Wealth Fund America Needs
items.desc: Two recent proposals to establish a new US sovereign wealth fund would fail to make good on a good idea, because neither plan would produce a fund nearly large enough to meet America’s mounting financing needs. But a different approach, funded by Treasury sales, could.

items.title: Trump’s Vanity Summit With Xi
items.desc: While expectations for the summit between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping were low, it was disappointing to watch them prioritize pageantry over substance. Trump’s cringe-worthy declarations of heartfelt admiration for Xi reflect his twisted sense that the trappings of power are power itself.

items.title: Human Rights and Populist Wrongs
items.desc: For the first time, all the UK’s political parties on the right favor withdrawing from the European Convention on Human Rights. But the story of the Hillsborough Law shows how human-rights laws, not least the ECHR, help ordinary people hold the state accountable for its costliest failings.

items.title: Is Another Eurozone Debt Crisis Looming?
items.desc: At a time when the cost of servicing sovereign debt is rising globally, France stands out as an especially fragile case. Its public debt-to-GDP ratio is edging up toward that of Greece on the eve of its sovereign-debt crisis, and the French political system seems unable to do anything about it.

items.title: Will AI Reverse the Renminbi’s Rise?
items.desc: In China, AI-driven productivity gains will most likely be in non-tradable services, which could push down relative prices and put downward pressure on the renminbi’s real exchange rate. To ensure that this does not also mean lower income and weaker demand, policymakers should ensure that the productivity dividend is broadly shared.

items.title: The Price of You
items.desc: As more people shop online, firms are increasingly setting individualized prices based on personal data, including purchase history, location, demographics, behavior, and biometric data. AI threatens to turbocharge such surveillance pricing, further widening the gap between privacy expectations and reality.

items.title: Investing in Brain Health
items.desc: Just as AI agents are mastering complex cognitive tasks, our own ability to perform the same tasks is eroding. Whether AI vindicates its boosters or fizzles out like the Metaverse craze of 2022, we will not fare well without a civilization-wide effort to rebuild the cognitive skills that make technological progress possible.

items.title: Europe Still Needs Molecules
items.desc: Not even the most effective European electrification strategy will eliminate the need for the molecules that fossil fuels provide. Given this, Europe must diversify its oil and gas supplies, maintain its refining capacity, and lock in decarbonization by building a hydrogen-energy industry at scale.

items.title: Energy Security in an Age of Disruption
items.desc: While there is no single prescription for energy security, strengthening “response capacity,” such as by establishing stockpiles, substituting sources, and diversifying suppliers, is essential. The point is not to eliminate vulnerabilities altogether, but to ensure that there are options when disruption arrives.
